summary:
Section 210 of the Penal Code criminalises male same-sex sexual activity. Anal or oral sex, whether between two men or between a man and a woman, is punishable as sodomy with up to fourteen years' imprisonment; other same-sex acts carry up to three years. Sex between women is not restricted by law. The penalties attach to sexual acts rather than to transgender identity as such.

As of 2024 Papua New Guinea has no legal recognition of transgender or gender-diverse identities. The sources state no transgender-specific criminal provision, identity-document rule, screening procedure, facilities rule, custody rule or healthcare restriction of any kind, so neither a documented legal exposure nor a documented legal protection specific to gender identity is available to a trans visitor.

Enforcement of the sodomy provisions is sporadic. No prosecutions directed at LGBTQ people were recorded in 2012. In 2015 a man charged with indecent acts between males pleaded guilty and received a suspended sentence with community service and mandatory counselling; in 2022 two men were arrested after having sex. In 2011 decriminalisation was stated not to be a priority, and in 2023 the government confirmed there was no intent to repeal the laws criminalising male homosexuality, arguing existing violence and abuse protections were sufficient.

Violence against LGBTQ people, including trans people, is documented. A 2011 study found police were one of the main sources of violence against men who have sex with men and trans people. In Port Moresby, gay men have been sexually abused, raped and beaten by police, with abuse commonly continuing even when reported, as victims are often framed as perpetrators. LGBTQ people experience rape and violence across the country, and many have fled to Hanuabada, a village on Port Moresby's outskirts described as a sanctuary where transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation. A 24-year-old gay man recounted being pelted with stones and bottles. Public views are mixed, with homophobia widespread and homosexuality more accepted in coastal areas than in the Highlands, though no statement on societal tolerance of transgender people specifically is sourced.

Transgender Papua New Guineans use the Tok Pisin word palopa, reportedly derived from the name of singer Jennifer Lopez, to refer to a cultural and traditional third gender. The Sambia recognise a traditional third gender, kwolu-aatmwol, literally 'male thing transforming into female thing'. The words lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender tend to carry heavy stigma, and LGBTQ persons report discrimination in daily life and struggle to find jobs.

The broader accountability climate bears on safety. HRW reported in 2009 that a mob stripped, beat with hot iron rods and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded over 50 sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008, with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations, sometimes linked to HIV deaths, were used to hide murders and mitigate sentences; and police routinely take no action. HRW's 2017 world report assessed that police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse.
tangentialFactors:
The Asian Development Bank's 'Assessment of the Legal Status of Sexual and Gender Minorities in 17 Countries in Asia and the Pacific', dated 17 May 2024, lists Papua New Guinea among the assessed countries, with keywords including decriminalization and SOGIESC inclusion.

The sorcery-accusation violence documented by HRW in 2009 is not trans-specific, but it evidences a climate in which accusations against individuals can draw mob violence with little police response, a context relevant to any visitor whose gender presentation attracts suspicion or hostility.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ Papua New Guineans report discrimination in daily life and difficulty finding jobs. Hanuabada village on Port Moresby's outskirts functions as a sanctuary where the gay community is accepted and transgender people live openly, while in Port Moresby gay and trans people are commonly raped or beaten, sometimes by police. Campaigners say attitudes shift with exposure to the LGBT community.

Transgender Papua New Guineans use the Tok Pisin term palopa for a cultural and traditional third gender; the Sambia recognise kwolu-aatmwol, a traditional third gender literally meaning 'male thing transforming into female thing'. The terms lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender carry heavy stigma.
outOfScopeNotes:
No region-specific or provincial legal instrument altering the national framework was identified in the sources; Hanuabada's tolerance is described as a social fact, not a legal one.

The sources do not document any trans-specific violence statistic with a denominator for Papua New Guinea, so no comparative rate can be stated. The 2011 study on police violence is cited without a sample size or period in the inventory.

Whether the sodomy provisions have ever been applied to conduct involving a transgender person specifically is not stated in the sources.
